restatements.text: Proposes an amendment to the California Constitution to add Section 4.5 to Article XIII A, upon a two-thirds vote of the Legislature and approval by voters.

Requires that, starting January 1, 2027, any special tax imposed, extended, or increased by a local government or by local voters via initiative must be approved by a two-thirds vote of the electorate, overriding certain other constitutional provisions and subject to specific existing exceptions.

Prohibits local governments, including local voters exercising initiative power, from imposing ad valorem taxes on real property, overriding certain other constitutional provisions and subject to a specific existing exception.
Defines "Local government" and "special tax" using the definitions found in Section 1 of Article XIII C.

evidence.why: Restricting the ability of local governments to levy special taxes without a supermajority reduces their taxing and spending authority.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. The measure amends the state constitution to require a two-thirds vote of the electorate for any local government (including via citizen initiative) to impose, extend, or increase special taxes. It also strictly prohibits local governments and electorates from imposing new ad valorem taxes on real property, with specified existing exceptions.

Direct costs include potential lost revenue for local governments due to the higher threshold for special taxes and the ban on ad valorem real property taxes. Opportunity costs involve public services or infrastructure projects that might not be funded if tax measures fail to reach the two-thirds threshold.

Property owners and taxpayers benefit from restricted local tax increases. Local governments and those who rely on locally funded public services or infrastructure bear the cost of reduced funding capacity.

Local governments may shift toward proposing general taxes or increasing fees and assessments that are not classified as special taxes or ad valorem property taxes. Proponents of special taxes will have to spend more time and resources on campaigns to achieve the two-thirds supermajority.

It addresses the perceived problem of local taxes, particularly those proposed via citizen initiative, being too easy to pass and increasing the tax burden on residents and property owners. The mechanism reaches this by imposing a strict two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes and banning ad valorem property taxes outright, though this may create a problem of underfunded local services.
A minority of voters (more than one-third) gains the power to block local special taxes. State constitutional authority is strengthened at the expense of local government and local initiative power.

It is empirically settled that supermajority requirements for tax measures lead to fewer taxes being passed and lower overall local government revenue, though the exact impact on service quality and alternative revenue generation (like fees) varies.

Administration costs are minimal as this acts as a legal restriction on what can be placed on a ballot and enacted. Some legal costs may arise if there are disputes over what constitutes a 'special tax'.
It is a constitutional amendment and can only be undone by another constitutional amendment approved by state voters.
